opening.headline: Although it appears that the model directly queries the DB, what actually happens is the round-trip flow of tool calls.
body: When a user asks, “Tell me the weather and schedule in Seoul today,” an answer containing the actual weather and schedule appears a few seconds later. Just looking at the screen, it looks like the model has direct access to the weather server and calendar. However, the model is only a model that creates text and does not connect to the network.

In this class, we will look at the principle of how a tool definition becomes the input text of a model, the round trip leading to a request, call, result, and answer, the schema and `tool_choice` for determining arguments, the format for returning results and errors, and the criteria for processing multiple calls in parallel or sequentially. Next, we will check the weather and schedule inquiry cases.

As of 2026-10: Claude Opus 5.5·Sonnet 5.5·Fable 5.1·Mythos 5.1 rejects any/tool in tool_choice with 400 error. Use auto and strict tool input validation, but strict does not enforce the call itself. The four-value comparison below is limited to models that support forced calls.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: It can explain the principle that tool definitions are passed as input text to the model, and the model only produces output in the form of the call.
Can describe the round-trip flow of tool calls (request, call, result, response) and agent loops
You can distinguish the difference between the basic keyword of JSON Schema and the `tool_choice` value.
Distinguish between parallel and sequential calls

screens.title: It looks like the model is querying the DB.
screens.lead:
Read on to compare what the user sees with what's actually happening. It's helpful to think about what the intermediate steps might be that aren't visible on screen.

As of 2026-10: Claude Opus 5.5·Sonnet 5.5·Fable 5.1·Mythos 5.1 rejects any/tool ​​in tool_choice with 400 error. Use auto and strict tool input validation, but strict does not enforce the call itself. The four-value comparison below is limited to models that support forced calls.

visual.alt: A scene showing a user question, a model, and an arrow with a question mark between the model and the DB.
labels: Please tell me the weather and schedule in Seoul today

paragraphs: The user asked, “Tell me the weather and schedule in Seoul today,” and after waiting a few seconds, the answer came back with the actual weather and actual schedule. When you look at the screen, it looks like the model has directly connected to the weather server and calendar DB and read the values.

However, a model is just a model that takes input text and produces output text. No ability to connect to a network or open a database. All the model knows is its learned knowledge and what is contained in this request.

So why are actual weather and schedules included in the answer? This means that somewhere between the model and the DB, someone performed a query and passed the results to the model. The question for this class is this. Who is doing what in the middle?
The answer lies in a round-trip construct called tool calls. Understanding the structure makes it clear where to look when designing for errors, delays, and security in tool connections.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If the model does not open the DB directly, where should the code that opens the DB be located? That location determines who is responsible for security and error handling.

screens.outro: Before opening up the invisible intermediate steps, let's first recall similar structures you know.

screens.title: think about it
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever seen a structure where the web server does not open the DB directly, but receives data through an API call?
items.answer: This is a structure where one system sends a request to another system and receives a response. The requesting party does not know the other party's inner thoughts and only communicates with messages in the agreed format. What the model does when calling a tool is similar to this: it writes down the object to be called and its arguments in the promised format and passes them on.

items.prompt: Do you know the RPC method that executes a function by passing the function name and arguments as JSON?
items.answer: In a remote procedure call, the caller sends the function name and arguments, and the recipient performs execution. In a tool call, the model creates a name and arguments as the caller, and execution is left to my application. The key is who is responsible for implementation.

items.prompt: How will the time change if I send two independent queries at the same time?
items.answer: If you do two queries one after the other, the time taken will be added up, and if you do them simultaneously, the time will be reduced to the slower one. It is only safe if the two queries do not affect each other. This criterion is the key to distinguishing between parallel and sequential calls.

screens.outro: Let's summarize the structure we came up with as a round trip of tool calls.

screens.title: The tool definition becomes the input text for the model.
screens.lead: The following article is a hypothetical example that simply depicts the input that the model actually receives. The actual format varies from provider to provider, but the principle is the same. Select a highlighted verse and explain what it does.

visual.alt: A flow in which the tool definition and user question are combined into one input that goes into the model, and the model outputs text in the form of a call.
labels: The app runs, pastes the results, and requests again.

data.text:
[Notice] The following tools are available. If you need a tool, print its name and arguments in a given format..  
[Tool Definition] get_weather - Retrieves the current weather in the specified city. Arguments: location (string, required)  
[User] Tell me the weather in Seoul today.  
[Model output] Call get_weather. The location is Seoul.  
[pause] stop_reason: tool_use

marks.span: [Tool Definition] get_weather - Retrieves the current weather in the specified city. Arguments: location (string, required)
marks.note: This article is all about how the model knows the tools. The API converts the name, description, and `input_schema` contained in the request's `tools` into text that the model can read, and prepends it to the input along with system instructions. The model doesn't see my code, it only reads this description and makes its choice. So the name and description will determine your choice. As the number of tools increases, the input becomes longer and the number of candidates to choose from increases, which is why selection becomes more difficult.

marks.span: If you need a tool, print its name and arguments in a given format.
marks.note: What the model does is still generate text. It just reads the input and creates the following text. Tool calls are possible because the provider trains the model to produce output in this format. The argument is created according to the shape of `input_schema`, so the more accurate the schema, the more stable the argument.

marks.span: [Model output] Call get_weather. The location is Seoul.
marks.note: This output is the identity of the `tool_use` block. The API organizes this output into the `id`, `name`, and `input` structures and returns it to the app. Up to this point, nothing has happened to the weather server. The sentence to call was simply made.

The model stops after writing a call request, and the response lists `stop_reason: tool_use` as the reason for stopping. The app looks at this value, runs the tool, and then sends the same conversation back with the results. This iteration is called the agent loop. It repeats as long as `stop_reason` is `tool_use`, and if it ends without a call, it can be considered the final answer. It may not be completed in one round trip.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the definition of a tool as input text, let's follow how the round trip follows step by step.

ext.title: Tool use with Claude - How tool use works

screens.title: Tool call round trip: request, call, result, answer
screens.lead: Let's take a step-by-step look at how one tool call goes round and round. Select the right arrow to follow the flow step by step.

visual.alt: A round-trip flow diagram of request, tool_use, execution, tool_result, and final answer between the app and the model.

steps.title: 1. Send tools and questions along with your request.
steps.body: The app sends the tool definition to `tools` along with the user question. For example, the name, description, and argument format of `get_weather` to query the weather are included. The model reads this definition and picks which tool to use.

steps.title: 2. Model returns tool_use
steps.body: Instead of producing an answer, the model returns a block of `tool_use` along with `stop_reason: tool_use`. The block contains `id` of the call, `name` of the tool, and `input` of the arguments. The model has only written a request to be called, but has not done anything yet.

steps.title: 3. My code runs the function
steps.body: The app finds a function matching `name`, executes it by passing `input` as an argument, and gets the result. It is my code at this stage that actually connects to the weather server or DB. It is also responsible for handling permissions, errors, and retries.

steps.title: 4. Send tool_result as user message
steps.body: The app sends `tool_result` appended with `tool_use_id` in the user message. `tool_use_id` is a value that matches the result of which call. In OpenAI, `function_call_output` and `call_id` play the same role.

steps.title: 5. The model produces the final answer
steps.body: The model reads the results returned and creates a final text answer to show to the user. The magic seen in the first question was the result of this back and forth between the app and the model. This round trip may be repeated several times if necessary.

screens.outro: Let's next look at the definition of a tool that makes this round trip possible.

screens.title: Tool schema: name, description, input_schema
screens.lead: Below is an example definition of a weather query tool. Read the line-by-line explanation on the right to see how the model utilizes this definition.

notes.note: `name` is the tool name. It must be within 128 characters including letters, numbers, underscores, and hyphens. This name becomes the name of the tool_use returned by the model, and the app uses this value to find a function to execute.

`description` is a description written in plain text. Write down in detail what you do, when you use it, and how it works. The model selects the tool based on this description, so if the description is poor, it may choose the wrong tool or not call it at all. The documentation recommends at least 3 to 4 sentences for each tool, noting that the description has the greatest impact on tool performance.

`input_schema` defines arguments as JSON Schema. Here, one string called location is required. The model creates input according to this schema. If you write the required items or types incorrectly, the call arguments will be misaligned.

`input_examples` is optional and can provide an example call. Helps the model follow the correct shape when the argument format is difficult. Each example must match `input_schema` or a 400 error will result. Examples are included in the prompt, so simple examples add about 20 to 50 tokens, and nested examples add about 100 to 200 tokens.

Gemini passes the function declaration to the tool, and the model returns a function call step. Although the names are different, the structure is the same in that it identifies the tool with three elements: name, description, and argument definitions.

screens.outro: Next, let's see how the app processes the call returned by the model and returns the result.

screens.title: How to read input_schema: JSON Schema basic vocabulary
screens.lead: The tool's arguments are written in a promised vocabulary called JSON Schema. Read the rows of the table from top to bottom to see how each keyword determines the shape of the argument.

data.caption: JSON Schema keywords frequently used in tool definitions
rows: Determine the type of value. There are string, number, integer, boolean, array, object, and null.
`location` is written as `"type": "string"`, and the outer part that binds the entire argument is written as `"type": "object"`.
Lists the names of the items an object can have and the schema for each item.
This will be a list of names of arguments the tool receives. The name is the key that the model uses for `input`.
A list of item names that must be included.
If omitted, only arguments for which the call will not be established are listed. In weather tools it is `"required": ["location"]`.
Restricts that the value must be one of a given list.
Closing out possible values, such as `"unit": {"type": "string", "enum": ["celsius", "fahrenheit"]}`, reduces erroneous values.
The value of the item is again `object`, or it takes multiple values of the same kind as `array` and `items`.
You get the attendee list from your scheduling tool as `{"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}}`, and so on.
This is a description attached to each item in the schema.
Write down the meaning and format of the arguments. This is the cue that the model reads when populating the values.
data.notes: The model reads this schema and produces `input` that matches the shape. A loose schema forces the model to guess the format, and closing candidates like `enum` leaves less room for guessing. Still, since `input` is a value generated by the model, it is safe to verify it one more time before running the app. MCP's `inputSchema` also uses the same JSON Schema.

screens.outro: Once you've defined the arguments, you also need to know how the app decides whether or not the model should use the tool.

screens.title: Decide how to use the tool with tool_choice
screens.lead: Move the slider to check the four values of `tool_choice` one by one. Each value determines whether the model uses a tool or not and who decides which tool to use.

stops.body: The model decides for itself whether to use the tool or not. This is the default value when defining and sending a tool. If the question can be answered without a tool, it will be answered immediately, and if a query is required, `tool_use` will be returned. This value is appropriate for context-sensitive requests, such as interactive services.

The model must use one of the provided tools, but it is up to the model to choose which tool to use. It is suitable for classification or routing where every input must be converted into a tool call. This value does not precede `tool_use` with an explanatory sentence.

If you give it a name like `{"type": "tool", "name": "get_weather"}`, your model will be sure to call that tool. It is suitable when you need structured output with a fixed shape and want to use a schema as an output format. Even in this case, there is no preceding explanatory sentence.

The model cannot use any tools. This is also the default when sending without defining a tool. Use this when you want to leave the list of tools in the request and have the player respond verbally without a call this turn.

screens.outro: Now that we have both definitions and selection methods, let's see what the call results look like.

screens.title: Result return format and error return
screens.lead: Select each tab to see the format for sending tool_result. Compare the differences between cases with results and cases with failure.

tabs.label: string
tabs.body: This is the simplest form. Send a string to `content` of `tool_result`. It is a basic form that pairs one call with one result. The longer the result, the more input the model must read, so it is recommended to include only the necessary information. The result of the call is indicated by pairing it with `tool_use_id`. If the result is short text, such as a weather query, this format is sufficient.

tabs.label: block list
tabs.body: In addition to strings, `content` can be sent as a list of nested content blocks or as a list of document blocks. The following formats can be used in blocks: text, image, document, and search_result. This format is used when a tool needs to return an image or document.

tabs.label: error
tabs.body: If the tool execution fails, notify us with `is_error: true` and a short description. Even if it fails, if you send it without the result, the call and result will not match. If you report errors in descriptive sentences, the model can understand the situation and provide appropriate guidance to the user.

tabs.label: No results
tabs.body: Please return the fact that there are no search results as an explanatory sentence rather than an empty value. A model that receives empty values ​​cannot tell whether the tool is broken or really has no results and can be misunderstood. Send something meaningful like “I don’t have any plans for that date.” Since zero search results and a search failure are completely different facts, the former should be reported as a general result and the latter as an error. This distinction determines the model's next actions.

screens.outro: Let's see what happens when there are multiple calls.

screens.title: Parallel and sequential calls
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare the difference between executing the same two calls in parallel and sequentially.

visual.alt: Illustration comparing the timeline length when running two tool calls in parallel and sequentially.

states.label: parallel
states.body: By default, a model can contain multiple `tool_use` blocks in one response. The API does not specify an execution order and can be executed both concurrently and sequentially. Read operations that are independent of each other can be run in parallel to reduce latency. The overall latency is reduced by the slower rather than the sum of the two hits. In either method, `tool_result` is sent one by one for each `tool_use` in one user message, and the `tool_result` block is placed before the text of the message. If you only want to take one call per turn, you can put `tool_choice` to `disable_parallel_tool_use: true`.

states.label: sequential
states.body: If there are side effects or order dependencies, sequential execution is safe. For example, if the second call depends on the results written by the first call, they cannot run concurrently. Since the API does not guarantee order, it is up to the app to maintain order. Even for calls that were not executed because the previous call failed, a result of `is_error: true` must be returned so that tool_result is paired with all tool_uses.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the standards, we will apply them to examples and explain them.

screens.title: Explanation: How weather and schedule requests are called in parallel
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process by which a request to “Tell me the weather in Seoul and my schedule tomorrow” is processed. Select the right arrow to follow step by step.

visual.alt: Schematic showing how the app, model, and two tools flow vertically and make parallel calls.
labels: Two tool_results in one user message

steps.title: 1. User request
steps.body: The user asks, “Tell me the weather in Seoul and my schedule tomorrow.” This question asks for two different pieces of information. Since the weather resides in the weather server and the schedule resides in the calendar, you need two tools. The app sends the definitions of both tools to the model in `tools`.

steps.title: 2. Model's response: two tool_use
steps.body: The model's response contains two `tool_use` in one turn: `get_weather`, `get_calendar`. The model decided that both pieces of information were needed, so it requested them all at once. Each block has a different `id`.

steps.title: 3. The app runs two queries simultaneously
steps.body: The app ensures that the two hits are independent of each other. Weather results are not required for calendar queries, both queries are read only and have no side effects. Therefore, it is safe to run them simultaneously.

steps.title: 4. Returns the result as one message
steps.body: The app sends two `tool_result`, each with `tool_use_id`, in one user message. Please note that the two results are not sent separately, but are sent together. Each tool_use must have a matching result.

steps.title: 5. The model combines the results
steps.body: The model combines the two results to create an answer like “It’s going to rain in Seoul tomorrow, so take an umbrella if you’re going to a morning meeting.” The user only sees one answer, but behind the scenes there are two hits and one composite.

steps.title: 6. Effect of parallelism
steps.body: Parallelism reduces latency to the slower rather than the sum of the two queries. The advantage of parallel execution is that the delay perceived by the user is reduced. However, this benefit can only be achieved when the two queries are independent.

screens.outro: Let's continue to figure out what to do if one fails.

screens.title: Commentary: What to do when a tool fails
screens.lead: The instructor compares two treatments for situations where a schedule lookup fails in the same request. Select the right arrow to cycle through incorrect processing, correct processing, and model response.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing the normal flow and the schedule inquiry failure flow left and right.
labels: Notifies that only the weather is provided and the schedule cannot be confirmed.

steps.title: 1. Situation: Schedule inquiry times out
steps.body: The weather query was successful, but the schedule query failed due to a timeout. Now the app must decide what to return to the model. Failure is common, so you should decide in advance how you will deal with it.

steps.title: 2. Incorrect processing: Send without results
steps.body: If you exclude `tool_result` from the failed call and only send the weather results, `tool_use` and `tool_result` will not match. This request is malformed because every `tool_use` must have `tool_result`. Additionally, the model has no way of knowing what was scheduled.

steps.title: 3. Sending an empty value as if it were a success is also dangerous
steps.body: There is also an option to send an empty string as a success result, but this is not recommended. The model may misunderstand that she has no schedule and reply, “I have no schedule today.” Failure and no results are two different things.

steps.title: 4. Correct handling: is_error and description
steps.body: Send `is_error: true` and `tool_result` with "Schedule service not responding." This way, the match is correct and the model knows correctly that the schedule query failed.

steps.title: 5. Model response
steps.body: The model may inform the user that it only reports the weather and does not have an itinerary. Users can make informed decisions rather than receiving incorrect information.

steps.title: 6. Retry policy is up to the app
steps.body: The app decides how many times to retry the schedule query. All you need to do is pass the results to the model. Even if you retry, if it ultimately fails, you will be notified with is_error as above.

screens.outro: Now let's summarize the entire lesson.

screens.title: Model makes request, app executes
screens.lead: Let's go back to the first question and summarize the structure of tool calls once and for all.

paragraphs: The first question I asked was that the model appears to query the database directly, but what actually happens? The answer is that the model just returns a structured request to call the tool without querying the database, and my application does the actual execution of the client tool I defined. Server tools like web_search are run by Anthropic's infrastructure and the results are returned in the same response.

The round trip flows in the following order: request, tool_use, execution of the app, tool_result, and final answer. The tool schema informs the model of the tool's usage and arguments through name, description, and input_schema. Multiple tool calls can occur in a single turn, and independent read calls can be executed in parallel. If there are order dependencies or side effects, sequential execution is safe.

For all tool_uses, the tool_result paired with tool_use_id is collected and returned in one message. Instead of omitting failures, we report is_error so the model can understand the situation. Since the app is running, the app is also responsible for permissions, errors, and retries. The person creating the app decides which tools to give the model and what each tool can do. This decision becomes the safety boundary for your service.

Tool results are also input text to the model. Since the model reads both tool definitions and results as the same input and decides its next action, it may try to follow statements that appear to be instructions mixed in the results. This is why the app must decide which tools to give and how much to trust the results.

Use this structure as a guideline when designing tools. All the model reads is the tool's name, description, and argument schema, and all it receives is the result sentence returned by the app. You can decide whether to use the tool or not with `tool_choice`.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The model only requests calls and does not execute them. The responsibility for executing the tools I define lies with my application.

glossary.def: A response block where the model requests a tool call. It has id, name, and input.
This is a block in which the app returns the results of tool execution to the model. Match the call with tool_use_id.
This is the part where the tool arguments are defined as JSON Schema. Determine the shape of arguments using keywords such as type, properties, required, and enum.
This is a request setting that determines whether the model will use a tool and which tool to use. It has four values: auto, any, tool, and none.
It is a repeat structure that runs the tool while stop_reason is tool_use, attaches the results, and requests it again.
Property of tool_result that indicates that the tool execution failed.

misconceptions.myth: The model directly queries the DB.
misconceptions.fact: The model only makes the call request, and the client tools I define are executed by my application. So the responsibility for permissions and error handling also lies with the app. Only server tools like web_search are run by Anthropic's infrastructure for you.

misconceptions.myth: Multiple calls should always be executed in parallel.
misconceptions.fact: The API does not dictate the order of execution. Parallel is advantageous for independent read operations, but sequential is safer if there are side effects or order dependence.

misconceptions.myth: For tools that fail, just omit the results.
misconceptions.fact: Every tool_use must have a tool_result. Failures should be signaled with is_error: true and a description so the model understands what happened.

misconceptions.myth: When you register a tool, the model knows the code of the function and executes it directly.
misconceptions.fact: All the model sees is text containing the tool's name, description, and argument schema. The code is not visible or executed. Parallel calls and execution order are also determined by the app, not the model.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The model does not query the DB directly. The tool definition is passed as input text, the model only returns a structured request in the form of a call, and the actual execution is done by my application.
The round trip flows in the following order: request, tool_use, app launch, tool_result, final answer, and repeat as long as stop_reason is tool_use.
The tool schema indicates its use and arguments through name, description, and input_schema, and tool_choice determines how the tool is used.
Multiple tool calls can occur in a single turn, and independent read calls can be executed in parallel.
For every tool_use, the tool_result paired with tool_use_id is collected and returned in one message, and failure is notified with is_error.
